Forthright

/FORTH-ryte/ - the stress falls on FORTH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Forthright means direct and honest in what one says.

The estimate was forthright: the mason listed what the wall would cost, what could go wrong, and which repairs could safely wait a decade.

Worked Example

Asked by the buyers what the house was really like in winter, the seller was forthright — the kitchen was cold, the lane flooded twice a year, and the furnace was on its last season.

Forthright describes speech that walks straight at the point. A tactful answer detours and a cagey one escapes; a forthright one arrives — direct, honest, and unafraid of costing its speaker something.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

plainspoken: Plainspoken is a habit of style — plain, everyday words with no jargon or ornament. Forthright is about substance: a forthright answer tells the hard truth even when the truth costs the speaker, and it can arrive in fancy language. A plainspoken person may still dodge the hard question.

outspoken: Outspoken people voice their opinions freely and unprompted, sometimes more often and more loudly than anyone asked. Forthright is narrower: it means answering what you are asked directly and honestly. The outspoken volunteer their views; the forthright deliver the truth a question was owed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

mealy-mouthed: afraid to say anything plainly

roundabout: approaches every point sideways

Where it sits · how blunt the truth-telling gets — direct → forthright → tactless

direct vs. forthright: Direct is milder than forthright — direct only promises no detours, while forthright adds honesty that may cost the speaker something.

tactless vs. forthright: Tactless goes further than forthright and falls off the good end of the ladder: the forthright speaker tells hard truths with care, while the tactless one tramples feelings without noticing.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — forth

Root — forth: straight out, onward (Old English)

Root — right

Root — right: direct, true (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Forthright is plain Old English carpentry: forth, 'straight onward,' joined to right, 'direct, true.' A forthright answer travels forth in a right line — no detour, no varnish. It is one of the few SAT-grade words whose parts are both everyday words you have known since childhood.

Use the root in a new word: forthcoming

Use the root in a new word: forthcoming: The agency was finally forthcoming about the delays, releasing the full schedule unprompted.

Word Choice

neutral / approving

Forthright praises directness and honesty in one word, and it nearly always compliments. Candor, taught in this same unit, is the matching noun. Blunt and tactless describe the same straightness after it starts to bruise — a person can be forthright and kind at once.
